lessons.title: Arduino Uno R3 Development
lessons.introduction: The classic 5V teaching board. Simple, predictable, and forgiving for beginners learning digital I/O, analogRead(), PWM, and basic robotics without complex voltage shifting.
objectives: Identify the MCU, architecture (8-bit AVR (ATmega328P)), and logic voltage (5V Logic) of Arduino Uno R3.
Configure Arduino IDE Boards Manager correctly for Arduino Uno R3.
Respect board-specific pin limits, ADC resolution, and variant differences.
conceptExplanation: The classic 5V teaching board. Simple, predictable, and forgiving for beginners learning digital I/O, analogRead(), PWM, and basic robotics without complex voltage shifting.
I/O pins operate at 5V (max ~20 mA recommended per pin, 40 mA absolute max). Do not connect 3.3V-only sensor logic lines directly without a level shifter.

Pin & Peripheral Highlights: 14 digital I/O pins (D0/D1 are shared with USB Serial — avoid using D0/D1 for LEDs/buttons while debugging). 6 hardware PWM pins marked with ~ (D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11). 6 analog inputs A0–A5 with 10-bit resolution (0 to 1023 representing 0V to 5V). External interrupts on D2 and D3; I2C on A4 (SDA) / A5 (SCL); SPI on D10–D13.
lessons.analogy: Just as diesel and electric vehicles share a steering wheel but have completely different drivetrains and voltages, different Arduino/ESP32 boards share C++ syntax while differing sharply in hardware specs.

lessons.title: Arduino Uno R4 Development
lessons.introduction: Keeps the familiar 5V Uno form factor while upgrading to a 32-bit 48 MHz ARM processor, 256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM, hardware CAN bus, and a true 12-bit DAC.
objectives: Identify the MCU, architecture (32-bit ARM Cortex-M4 (Renesas RA4M1)), and logic voltage (5V Logic) of Arduino Uno R4.
Configure Arduino IDE Boards Manager correctly for Arduino Uno R4.
Respect board-specific pin limits, ADC resolution, and variant differences.
conceptExplanation: Keeps the familiar 5V Uno form factor while upgrading to a 32-bit 48 MHz ARM processor, 256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM, hardware CAN bus, and a true 12-bit DAC.
Still 5V logic on GPIO pins, but per-pin current sourcing/sinking is lower (~8 mA recommended on RA4M1) than the older ATmega328P! Always use resistors and transistors/drivers for loads.

Pin & Peripheral Highlights: Available in two official editions: Uno R4 Minima (USB-C, SWD) and Uno R4 WiFi (adds ESP32-S3 co-processor + 12x8 LED Matrix + Qwiic I2C). Supports 10-bit default ADC or higher resolution via analogReadResolution(14). Pin A0 doubles as a true 12-bit Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC). AVR-specific register code (like TCCR1A or PORTB) will NOT compile on Uno R4.
lessons.analogy: Just as diesel and electric vehicles share a steering wheel but have completely different drivetrains and voltages, different Arduino/ESP32 boards share C++ syntax while differing sharply in hardware specs.

lessons.title: Arduino Nano Family Development
lessons.introduction: The Arduino Nano name covers a breadboard-friendly form factor spanning very different microcontrollers. Never assume two Nano boards share the same voltage, core, or bootloader.
objectives: Identify the MCU, architecture (Multiple MCUs across Nano variants), and logic voltage (5V (Classic/Every) or 3.3V (Nano 33/ESP32)) of Arduino Nano Family.
Configure Arduino IDE Boards Manager correctly for Arduino Nano Family.
Respect board-specific pin limits, ADC resolution, and variant differences.
conceptExplanation: The Arduino Nano name covers a breadboard-friendly form factor spanning very different microcontrollers. Never assume two Nano boards share the same voltage, core, or bootloader.
CRITICAL: Nano Classic and Nano Every use 5V logic, whereas Nano 33 IoT, Nano 33 BLE, and Nano ESP32 use STRICT 3.3V logic. Applying 5V to a 3.3V Nano pin can permanently destroy the chip.

Pin & Peripheral Highlights: Nano Classic (ATmega328P) has A6 and A7 as analog-input-only pins — they cannot be used with digitalWrite(). Many clone Nano Classic boards use a CH340 USB-to-Serial chip and the 'ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)' option. Nano Every (ATmega4809) offers 48 KB Flash and 6 KB SRAM at 5V with a separate hardware Serial1 on D0/D1. Nano ESP32 uses 3.3V logic, USB-C, and Arduino pin numbering vs GPIO numbering options.
lessons.analogy: Just as diesel and electric vehicles share a steering wheel but have completely different drivetrains and voltages, different Arduino/ESP32 boards share C++ syntax while differing sharply in hardware specs.

rules: Nano Classic (ATmega328P) has A6 and A7 as analog-input-only pins — they cannot be used with digitalWrite().
Many clone Nano Classic boards use a CH340 USB-to-Serial chip and the 'ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)' option.
Nano Every (ATmega4809) offers 48 KB Flash and 6 KB SRAM at 5V with a separate hardware Serial1 on D0/D1.

lessons.title: Arduino Mega 2560 Development
lessons.introduction: Built for large-scale 5V robotics projects that outgrow the Uno's pin count and memory. Offers 256 KB Flash, 8 KB SRAM, 54 digital pins, 16 analog inputs, and 4 hardware serial ports.
objectives: Identify the MCU, architecture (8-bit AVR (ATmega2560)), and logic voltage (5V Logic) of Arduino Mega 2560.
Configure Arduino IDE Boards Manager correctly for Arduino Mega 2560.
Respect board-specific pin limits, ADC resolution, and variant differences.
conceptExplanation: Built for large-scale 5V robotics projects that outgrow the Uno's pin count and memory. Offers 256 KB Flash, 8 KB SRAM, 54 digital pins, 16 analog inputs, and 4 hardware serial ports.

5V logic like the Uno R3, but do not draw high total current across all 54 pins simultaneously (respect total port and Vcc/GND current limits; power motors and servos from an external supply with shared GND).

Pin & Peripheral Highlights: 4 independent hardware UARTs: Serial (USB), Serial1 (18/19), Serial2 (16/17), Serial3 (14/15) — eliminates fragile SoftwareSerial. 15 PWM pins (D2–D13 and D44–D46) for controlling multiple servos and motor drivers. SPI pins differ from Uno R3: MISO=50, MOSI=51, SCK=52, SS=53. I2C pins are D20 (SDA) and D21 (SCL).

lessons.title: ESP32 Family Development
lessons.introduction: A high-performance 3.3V microcontroller family with integrated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Different ESP32 silicon variants have distinct CPU cores, pinouts, USB peripherals, and ADC rules.
objectives: Identify the MCU, architecture (32-bit Xtensa LX6/LX7 or RISC-V (variant-dependent)), and logic voltage (3.3V Logic ONLY) of ESP32 Family.
Configure Arduino IDE Boards Manager correctly for ESP32 Family.
Respect board-specific pin limits, ADC resolution, and variant differences.
conceptExplanation: A high-performance 3.3V microcontroller family with integrated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Different ESP32 silicon variants have distinct CPU cores, pinouts, USB peripherals, and ADC rules.
STRICT 3.3V LOGIC ONLY. Never connect 5V sensor outputs (such as an HC-SR04 Echo pin powered at 5V) directly to an ESP32 GPIO without a voltage divider or logic level shifter.

Pin & Peripheral Highlights: On classic ESP32-WROOM-32, GPIO 34, 35, 36, and 39 are INPUT-ONLY and have no internal pull-up resistors. Avoid pulling boot strapping pins (e.g., GPIO 0, 2, 12, 15 on classic ESP32) to the wrong state at reset. 12-bit ADC returns 0–4095 instead of Arduino Uno's 0–1023. Use analogWrite() in Arduino-ESP32 v3.x or LEDC APIs; note that ESP32-C3 is single-core RISC-V while ESP32-S3 is dual-core Xtensa LX7 with native USB.
lessons.analogy: Just as diesel and electric vehicles share a steering wheel but have completely different drivetrains and voltages, different Arduino/ESP32 boards share C++ syntax while differing sharply in hardware specs.

syntaxExplanation.summary: ESP32 analogRead() uses 12-bit resolution (0–4095) and 3.3V reference; stick to ADC1 pins (e.g., GPIO 32–35 on WROOM-32) when using Wi-Fi.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
// ESP32-WROOM-32: 12-bit ADC on ADC1 pin (GPIO 34, input-only)
const int SENSOR_PIN = 34; // ADC1 channel (safe with Wi-Fi)
rules: On classic ESP32-WROOM-32, GPIO 34, 35, 36, and 39 are INPUT-ONLY and have no internal pull-up resistors.
Avoid pulling boot strapping pins (e.g., GPIO 0, 2, 12, 15 on classic ESP32) to the wrong state at reset.
12-bit ADC returns 0–4095 instead of Arduino Uno's 0–1023.
